rows.reason: Three towers spaced on a line give every flat a fairer share of the sea than four crowded diamonds.
rows.quote: Three well-spaced towers are generous; four identical diamonds are greedy and every one of them looks into its neighbour.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Four identical diamond-set slabs. The 45-degree rotation opens corners to the sea, but the central tower sits in the view cone of the southern pair, so view equity is poor. The inner corners face each other across roughly 25 m. The extrusions never change, so the silhouette reads as a cluster of sticks.

floor_changes.direction: all four towers, stepping in on the west and sea faces
floor_changes.why: Lets the rear towers see the sea past the front ones and makes the cluster more slender.

floor_changes.direction: central tower rotated off the diagonal toward the Arabian Sea to the west
floor_changes.why: Breaks the corner-to-corner overlooking between the centre tower and the SW tower.

floor_changes.amount: sculpted sloped crown, varied heights of +/-12 m between towers
floor_changes.why: Gives a Hadid-like family silhouette instead of four identical tops.

win1.whats_wrong: Three towers on a clean diagonal line, which is much better for equity and separation. The plates barely rotate, though. The line runs SW-NE, so the middle tower still takes the flank view of its neighbours, and the sea-facing faces are flat.

floor_changes.direction: progressively toward the sea to the west
floor_changes.amount: about 2 degrees every 5 floors, up to 15 degrees
floor_changes.why: Turns more living rooms to the sea as the towers clear the low city.
Widens the sea arc for corner flats.
Varies the silhouette and gives the middle tower views over its neighbours.

rows.reason: The rounded plates capture wider arcs and sit better against the heritage context.
rows.quote: Neither building yet speaks to the street; B at least has the manners of a curve.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Two square extrusions with no gesture toward the Thames. They add nothing to the street: no podium relationship with the medieval lanes and a blunt, identical skyline presence. The west tower half-blocks the eastern one's river diagonal.

floor_changes.amount: 4-storey colonnaded base following the lane geometry
floor_changes.why: Rebuilds the public realm instead of leaving two towers standing on a plaza.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the south and SE
floor_changes.why: Points the long faces at the river and Tower Bridge.

floor_changes.amount: one tower 15 m lower, with a sloped top
floor_changes.why: Gives the skyline a sculptural identity instead of twins.

win1.whats_wrong: The rounded squircles are softer and read better against the Tower of London, and the rounded corners widen the view arcs. It is still a pair of undifferentiated tubes with no base and no response to the river side.

floor_changes.direction: street frontage to the north and west
floor_changes.amount: 12 m high base with an arcade
floor_changes.why: Anchors the towers to the street pattern.

floor_changes.direction: all faces, more on the south
floor_changes.why: Gives a more sculpted top that opens toward the Thames.
Evidence from the aerial: a staggered pair reads better against the Tower of London and the rear tower sees over.

rows.reason: A has proportion and the beginnings of a stepped language; B is two anonymous tubes.
rows.quote: A is almost a composition; B is a pair of pencils.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Three chamfered slim towers with a faint stagger, which is a more Safdie-like sensibility. In a Midtown canyon, though, the towers sit about 25 m apart with a small, repetitive offset that achieves neither gardens nor real views. The southern tower is jammed against the site edge.

floor_changes.direction: corners facing away from the sister towers
floor_changes.why: Adds outdoor space and breaks the direct overlooking between the towers.

floor_changes.direction: toward the open avenue to the east
floor_changes.why: Pushes plates out past the neighbouring masonry toward long views.
Gives an MVRDV-like stepped trio.

win1.whats_wrong: Only two rounded tubes, and the north tower is buried behind grey neighbours. The separation is better, but the form is generic and ignores the grid and the setback heritage.

floor_changes.amount: base matching the 30 m cornice line
floor_changes.why: Respects the Manhattan street wall.
Frees views past the adjacent towers.

rows.reason: The twist gives the view and the skyline presence.
rows.quote: B dances; if we bundle the floors, it can dance on a budget.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A chamfered square that tapers very slightly and is otherwise an inert prism. Every face gets the same glass, with no shading response to the south sun, and nothing on the plate says where the Barbican gardens are.

floor_changes.amount: 1.2 m deep fins and balconies every floor
floor_changes.why: Climate shading while keeping the repetitive plate.

floor_changes.direction: toward the green spaces to the SW
floor_changes.why: Frames the park views.

win1.whats_wrong: The twisting triangle is a Nouvel/Zaha gesture that gives the tower an identity, and the rotating vertices sweep across the park. Every floor is different, which hurts repetition, and the upper plate still grows wide.

floor_changes.amount: rotate in 4-floor blocks of about 7 degrees
floor_changes.why: Keeps the twist legible while repeating the formwork.
A finer crown and better proportion.
Usable corner rooms and less wind.

rows.reason: At least B has edges for balconies; A is a dumb box looking into a wall.
rows.quote: A looks straight into its neighbour's office; B has barely noticed the Thames.

win1.whats_wrong: A square slab in the middle of a triangle, hemmed in by that huge grey tower directly in front of the outlook side. Flats on that face stare straight into it. There are no balconies, the small notches look like leftovers, and there is no bold move.

floor_changes.direction: south toward the Thames, away from the adjacent tower
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space per flat and a lift above the neighbour.

floor_changes.direction: rotate away from the tall neighbour to the east
floor_changes.why: Stops the face-to-face overlooking.

hyb2.whats_wrong: The elongated octagon rotates a little and the tops of the plates step, which gives balcony edges. The rotation is timid, the long face still faces the neighbour, and the plan loses efficiency at the corners.

floor_changes.why: Big BIG-style terraces for real outdoor space.
The wobble costs efficiency without buying views.
Clears the neighbouring roofline.

rows.reason: Same cost, better turned to the sea.
rows.quote: B is the one I can sell; now give it a twist people will remember.

win1.whats_wrong: A clean square on a triangular site: very buildable and isolated from its neighbours, but plain. It does not turn toward the Arabian Sea to the west or Shivaji Park to the NE. It reads as a standard Mumbai tower.

floor_changes.direction: toward the sea to the NW
floor_changes.why: Sea-facing living rooms.
A marketable skyline identity.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Rotating the plate about 12 degrees toward the sea helps and costs nothing to build. It is still just a box, with no sculpture for a sales brochure.

floor_changes.amount: 1 degree per floor, grouped every 3 floors
floor_changes.why: Identity and more sea arc.
Premium sea-facing units.

rows.reason: A has poise and B has equity; each needs something the other has.
rows.quote: Two respectable towers; I would twist B a little and round off A.

win1.whats_wrong: A slender square rotating gently through its height. It is elegant, but the rotation is slight and lacks conviction. The lower floors face the rail and retail sheds, so those flats get a lesser view.

floor_changes.direction: toward the rail and retail to the south
floor_changes.why: Takes lesser-view floors out of the housing mix, for equity.
More even corner flats all the way round.

hyb2.whats_wrong: The rounded triangle is the same at every floor. It is equitable in all directions and calm beside the docks, but monotonous. The flat side facing SW loses the dock view.

floor_changes.why: Refines the top.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park and docks to the north
floor_changes.why: Aligns the long curve with the best view.

rows.reason: The twist is more composed; add loggias and it wins.
rows.quote: B turns to the harbour gracefully; A fidgets.

win1.whats_wrong: A stepped, jittering stack on the harbour edge. The floors shift and rotate enough to create terrace edges toward the water, and it is well away from its neighbours. The jitter looks nervous rather than purposeful next to Battery Park, and it gives no terraces on the harbour side specifically.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the SW
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space facing the water.
Calms the street side and the heritage edge.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A clean twist of about 45 degrees. It is elegant and sweeps the harbour, but it offers no balconies, and the twist turns some faces back toward the towers.

floor_changes.why: Outdoor space without breaking the twist.
Relates to the park and the heritage edge.

rows.reason: The chamfers and shifting edges give slightly more outdoor opportunity.
rows.quote: The render shows a wall; data before form, so first I'd move away from it.

hyb2.whats_wrong: The outlook-side aerial is completely blocked by a tall neighbour; the evidence says this tower stares into a wall. The chamfered octagon with slight shifted floor edges gives little outdoor space.

floor_changes.direction: away from the tall tower to the SE, toward the open NW
floor_changes.why: Puts terraces where the view is open.
Reduces overlooking.

win1.whats_wrong: A square with a minor rotation and varying size. It is just as hemmed in, with flat faces that give no balconies, and the necking at mid height looks accidental.

floor_changes.why: Studio Gang-style balconies with outdoor space.
Skyline identity.

rows.reason: A is slimmer and more repeatable; B is stubby.
rows.quote: A repeats well, but give it gardens or it's just an office tower with beds.

win1.whats_wrong: A very efficient, slender rotated square: repeatable and cheap. It has no outdoor space at all, and it faces a midblock of towers on two sides.

floor_changes.why: Outdoor space without losing repetition.

floor_changes.direction: toward the avenue to the east
floor_changes.why: Views past the neighbours.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A fat slab, lower and wider, with its long face facing the neighbours at close range. There is no outdoor space and the proportion is stubby.

floor_changes.amount: narrow by 6 m and add 30 m of height
floor_changes.why: Better proportion and less overlooking.
Outdoor space.

rows.reason: Both options are the same scheme. I'd sell either one only after the plates are rotated to the water.
rows.quote: Two boxes, same scheme twice. Turn them to the harbour and then we can talk price per foot.

win1.whats_wrong: Two identical square extrusions sitting on the site like twin shoeboxes. The plates don't rotate toward the Hudson and harbour to the west and south-west, so half the flats end up facing the inland towers to the east. The rear tower's west face looks straight into the front tower's east face at every level. At ground there's nothing: no podium edge, no plaza facing the esplanade.

floor_changes.amount: 4-storey retail/lobby podium on the full west frontage
floor_changes.why: Give the street and esplanade an active edge and sell the base.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the SW
floor_changes.why: Every flat gets a diagonal water view, not just the west stack.

floor_changes.direction: rear (NE) tower away from the front tower
floor_changes.why: Stop the living rooms facing each other at 60 m.
Premium penthouses and a skyline marker.

hyb2.whats_wrong: I can't tell it apart from A. Same twin squares, same axis, same heights. Everything I said about A applies here: no view equity, the towers face each other, and there's no public realm.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the SW
floor_changes.why: Diagonal water views for the rear units.

floor_changes.direction: NE tower pushed further into the east corner
floor_changes.why: More separation, less overlooking.
Public realm.

rows.reason: A has the better proportion and a cleaner build. B's rotation hints at better views but gives away height and slenderness.
rows.quote: A is the elegant one. B has an idea, but it hasn't committed to it.

win1.whats_wrong: It's a slender rounded-square cylinder with a light taper. The proportion is good and it sits well in the cluster, but it's a neutral object. The river is to the north and nothing in the form reaches for it, and the south flats get the neighbouring slab towers at close range.

floor_changes.direction: with the plate shifting north toward the Thames
floor_changes.why: Slimmer head and more river-facing corners.

floor_changes.direction: south-east corner facing the adjacent towers
floor_changes.why: Cut the oblique overlooking from the slabs next door.
Resolve the top.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Same cylinder, but the plate rotates and deforms floor by floor, and I like that in principle. It's lower, though (about 209 m against 234 m), so the proportion is squatter. The wobble reads as nervous rather than deliberate, and the slab-edge variation will cost you.

floor_changes.amount: add about 6 floors to reach roughly 230 m
floor_changes.why: Get the slenderness back.

floor_changes.direction: make it a single continuous rotation toward the river to the N
floor_changes.why: Read as one gesture, repeatable formwork.

rows.reason: A's rotation reads as one clear move on the skyline. B undoes its own twist.
rows.quote: A is at least trying to be a sculpture. Push it harder.

win1.whats_wrong: A square plate slowly rotating up the height. Visibly shifted slabs give it a sculptural stack, which I like, but the rotation is small and ends without a crown. For the City, next to St Paul's sightlines, a flat top is a missed identity moment.

floor_changes.direction: rotating toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: A stronger skyline identity, and the top floors face the river.
A signature top.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Same logic, but it rotates the other way and goes back toward orthogonal at the top, so the gesture dies. From the outlook side it reads as a straight prism with a slightly rippled edge.

floor_changes.direction: one consistent direction toward the river S
floor_changes.why: Make the twist legible.
Identity.

rows.reason: B's bolder rotations make overhangs that can actually become gardens.
rows.quote: B is almost a stack of villages. Now carve the gardens in.

win1.whats_wrong: There are three stacked blocks, each rotated, and the shifts leave ledges. That's close to the right idea, but the ledges are thin and accidental rather than usable terraces. It's also a chunky 137 m tower dropped into low-rise streets with no transition. The plate is big and deep, which means dark flats.

floor_changes.direction: toward the docks to the S/SW
floor_changes.amount: 3 m terrace at each block shift, every 8 floors
floor_changes.why: Give real outdoor rooms where the blocks rotate.

floor_changes.direction: to the street wall on the north
floor_changes.why: Meet the heritage street scale.
Lighten the head.

hyb2.whats_wrong: The rotations are more pronounced, and the diamond-on-plan lower floors turning to a square above give crisper overhangs, which is better material for balconies. The heritage edge still gets nothing, and neither scheme has a single garden.

floor_changes.direction: on the corners that overhang each rotation
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space for each flat.
Context.

rows.reason: B's rotation starts to negotiate with its neighbours. A just stands there.
rows.quote: B has the gentler manner, but both are shy. A tower here has to lean into its gaps.

win1.whats_wrong: The small square plate has slight floor-by-floor jitter. It's hemmed in by much taller towers to the east and a big slab to the south, so the lower half looks straight into walls. It sits in the middle of a generous site and wastes the hexagonal envelope.

floor_changes.direction: toward the open park and water to the SE
floor_changes.why: Slip past the adjacent towers and toward the open side.

floor_changes.direction: toward the dock to the S
floor_changes.why: Upper floors clear the neighbours.
Identity, in a Nouvel way.

hyb2.whats_wrong: It's the same small tower, rotated roughly 15 degrees. That rotation angles the glass away from the neighbour to the east, which helps. It still hides in the canyon, and the height limit isn't used to break above the neighbours.

floor_changes.why: Rise above the nearest roofline.

floor_changes.direction: away from the cylindrical tower to the NE
floor_changes.why: Privacy.

rows.reason: The two are almost the same. Both are too short and have no balconies.
rows.quote: A gentle shape, but it has forgotten the sun and the sky. Give it another 90 metres and balconies.

win1.whats_wrong: A soft rounded plate with light rotation. It stops at about 140 m in a canyon of 200 m-plus towers when 235 m is allowed, so the lower two-thirds see only facades. There are no balconies or shading. Round glass drums in New York summers overheat.

floor_changes.why: Get above the surrounding towers to the water.

floor_changes.direction: on the S and W for shade
floor_changes.amount: recessed 2.5 m loggias on alternate floors
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space and summer shading.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the W
floor_changes.why: Terraces with the view.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Practically the same as A, just a softer, slightly squarer plate. It has the same height deficit and the same absence of outdoor rooms.

floor_changes.why: Views.

floor_changes.direction: toward the water to the W/SW
floor_changes.amount: 2 m balcony band every floor on that side
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space with shading overhangs.

rows.reason: They are the same box.
rows.quote: Same extrusion twice. Rotate it or stop wasting my time.

win1.whats_wrong: A plain rectangular extrusion, efficient and dumb. The long faces point N and S, but the water is W and E, so the best elevations are the narrow ones. It sits flush against taller neighbours on its east side. There's no plan variation, but at least it's cheap.

floor_changes.direction: long axis toward the harbour to the S/SW
floor_changes.why: Put the wide elevation on the water.
Free floor area.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Identical to A. I have nothing new to say about it.

floor_changes.why: Views.
No point glazing a wall.

rows.reason: B's final rotation turns the widest face to the north outlook. That's a marginal win, if engineered.
rows.quote: Both are slim enough. B's head is prettier, so step the twist and build it.

win1.whats_wrong: A slender triangular plate twisting through the height, with good proportion at about 280 m. The twist is steady, but the plates shrink little, so the top feels blunt. A triangle also wastes plan corners, and every floor is different for the curtain wall.

floor_changes.direction: toward Central Park to the N
floor_changes.why: A finer spire.
Usable corner rooms and less wind vortex.
Repeatable panels, like Safdie's modular logic.

hyb2.whats_wrong: It's the same twisting triangle, starting from a different orientation and ending in a wider inverted triangle at the top. That gives a nicer crown flare, but it's top-heavy structurally.

floor_changes.why: Avoid flaring the crown against wind.
Repetition.

rows.reason: Both are the same in substance. A rotates slightly, B has rounder corners, and neither matters much.
rows.quote: Buildable, both. Separate them a little more and step down to the street.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Two chamfered square towers on a triangular site with a slight rotation. It's easy to build. The two towers are close on the diagonal and face each other, and neither steps toward the lower heritage streets to the north-west.

floor_changes.direction: west tower away from the NE tower
floor_changes.why: Privacy between the towers.
Match the terrace heights.

win1.whats_wrong: The same arrangement with softer rounded plates and no rotation. It's cleaner and just as repetitive, with the same tower-to-tower overlooking.

floor_changes.direction: W tower toward the SW apex
floor_changes.why: More separation.
A step toward the older fabric.

rows.reason: A's cutouts at least start an identity and give some shade.
rows.quote: A has the germ of a character. B is just a column.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A square plate with small corner cutouts and slight shifts. That creates a few notches, which help identity a little, but they're too timid to shade or to frame the Thames to the south. The west glass is unshaded.

floor_changes.why: Shaded view terraces.
Skyline identity.

win1.whats_wrong: A plain rotated square extrusion. It's clean and cheap, with no identity and no shading.

floor_changes.why: Silhouette.
Shade the afternoon sun.

rows.reason: A at least begins to turn and carve. B does nothing for any flat.
rows.quote: A starts a conversation with the city; B is a filing cabinet. I want every flat to have its garden corner.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A barely-there chamfer at the NW corner on the lower floors and a small rotation at the very top. The crown twist hints at the rivers, but the shaft is still a closed box with no shading, no outdoor rooms, and the north and south neighbours look straight in.

floor_changes.direction: NW and SE corners, toward the river glimpses
floor_changes.amount: double-height loggias 4 m deep every 3 floors
floor_changes.why: Gives every flat a corner outlook and outdoor room while cutting solar gain

floor_changes.direction: clockwise toward the Hudson to the west
floor_changes.amount: about 1 degree per floor, reaching 25 degrees
floor_changes.why: Lets the rotation build up gradually instead of being a surprise at the top, so faces slide past the towers next door
Shared view equity for the flats that sit lower

win1.whats_wrong: A plain square extrusion, the same at every floor. Nothing responds to sun or water, and every face is equally exposed to the Midtown walls around it.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river corridors to the W and E
floor_changes.why: Aims the diagonals down the gaps between the towers

floor_changes.amount: deep fins or balconies of 1.5 m
floor_changes.why: Shading, and a screen against the neighbours

rows.reason: A has better proportion and silhouette. The overlooking between the two towers can be fixed with a splay.
rows.quote: Two slender shafts, yes, but let them turn away from each other. Right now they are staring.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Two very slender chamfered pencils on a podium, which is elegant. But the plates are identical all the way up, the two towers face each other across the diagonal, and neither leans toward the East River.

floor_changes.direction: north tower toward the NW, south tower toward the E and the river
floor_changes.why: Stops the long faces from looking into each other
Finishes the slender reading and keeps wind load down

floor_changes.amount: 2 m bay window pods every 4 floors
floor_changes.why: Captures the river and adds Safdie-style shading and terraces

win1.whats_wrong: One diamond-oriented square rising 300 m. There is no overlooking between towers, but it is stocky beside A's pencils and completely inert.

floor_changes.amount: about 20% plate reduction by the top
floor_changes.why: At 300 m it needs to lighten as it rises
Reduces vortex shedding and widens corner views

rows.reason: The rotation buys privacy and outlook at almost no cost to efficiency.
rows.quote: B is the same kit of parts, just rotated smarter. It is cheap to build and easier to sell.

hyb2.whats_wrong: Four identical square pins on a grid, with the centre and north towers lined up on the same axis, so the flats look into each other. The plans are efficient, but the scheme ignores the docks and has no shading.

floor_changes.direction: centre tower rotated toward the dock to the SE
floor_changes.why: Breaks the north-south alignment in which the flats face each other
Solar control without losing floor area

win1.whats_wrong: Rotating the plates about 30 degrees gets the corners pointing outward and cuts down direct face-to-face views. It is still four similar sticks at the same height, and the skyline is monotonous.

floor_changes.amount: up to the full 185 m, about 8 floors more than the others
floor_changes.why: Varies the heights into a cluster silhouette and lifts views over One Canada Square's neighbours
Good for the leasing story and it activates the ground

rows.reason: Repetition wins, and A is the easier base to terrace toward the sea.
rows.quote: Give me one typical floor and a terrace every six. Everyone sees the sea, and the contractor stays sane.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A rotated square that barely changes from floor to floor. It is repeatable and buildable, but the sea side gets no more than a flat face, and the flats on the east side lose the Arabian Sea entirely.

floor_changes.why: Gives the rear flats a sea view over the ones in front, the way Safdie stacks units
Sea view equity for the corner units and cross-ventilation

win1.whats_wrong: A slim chamfered plate with a slight twist. It is more elegant, but the twist means every floor is different, and the narrow plate still leaves the east-facing units with the city rather than the sea.

floor_changes.why: Typical floors, so repetition and formwork reuse

floor_changes.amount: about 4 m of offset in total
floor_changes.why: More sea glazing on the upper units

rows.reason: A is calmer and more respectful of context. B's twist is clever, but the result is bulky.
rows.quote: B reaches for the park with its shoulders. A, turned 15 degrees, would do it with grace.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A generous chamfered octagon that tapers gently as it rises, which is refined. Its broad faces are square to the park but not to the sea to the west, and with the plate that deep the core zone is inefficient.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward Shivaji Park and the sea to the NW
floor_changes.why: Aligns the frontage with the two prime outlooks

floor_changes.direction: the street edge facing the precinct
floor_changes.why: Respects the Art Deco and heritage street rhythm of Dadar

win1.whats_wrong: A rectangular slab that twists about 20 degrees toward the park. The long face captures more outlook, but the corners are hard and the slab silhouette is bulky against the low heritage fabric.

floor_changes.why: Softens the MAD-like flow and reduces how bulky the tower reads
Lighter crown over the precinct

rows.reason: B's rotation reads the plaza and the long axis better. The base can be fixed.
rows.quote: Hold the street at the bottom, then let it turn. And give me verandahs, not glass.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A slim rectangle that drifts slowly clockwise as it rises. It sits well back from the street on a triangular plaza site but does nothing for the plaza, and there are no verandahs or deep reveals.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park plaza to the E
floor_changes.amount: an open, shaded arcade 3 floors deep
floor_changes.why: Doshi-like threshold space for the public realm
Shade, outdoor space, and a buffer against the neighbours looking in

win1.whats_wrong: A more pronounced rotation toward the triangle's long axis opens the upper floors toward the plaza. But the base floor sits hard on the street, and the rotation leaves awkward residual corners.

floor_changes.why: Holds the street wall at the base
Terraces over the open space

rows.reason: A has an identity, and its twisting faces avoid the neighbours.
rows.quote: A moves; B stands there. Just smooth that first turn.

win1.whats_wrong: A strong twisting slab. It rotates about 90 degrees over the height, which is sculptural, and faces slide past the neighbours. But the twist is jerky between floors 6 and 17, and the tower still lands clumsily on the street.

floor_changes.amount: 0 degrees, starting the twist at floor 17
floor_changes.why: Lets a street-aligned base meet the public realm
Zaha-like fluid continuity, and it sheds wind

hyb2.whats_wrong: A static square rotated diagonally in a triangular site. It is safe and buildable but has no form, no shading and nothing at street level.

floor_changes.direction: clockwise toward the Hudson to the W
floor_changes.why: Rotates the faces toward water and away from the walls
Street life

rows.reason: Both images show the same tower, so there is nothing to choose between them.
rows.quote: You showed me the same box twice. Neither one earns a place on the City skyline.

win1.whats_wrong: A rotated square extrusion, identical from floor 6 to floor 57, set diagonally so the corners face the Thames. It has no skyline identity, and there is no shading or verandah at all.

floor_changes.why: Correa-style open-to-sky spaces, and a signature for the skyline
Gives the top a sculpted profile among the City cluster

hyb2.whats_wrong: Identical to A in every image: same plates, same massing. It has the same failings.

floor_changes.why: MVRDV-style pixel stacking to break up the box and shade the glass

rows.reason: B is better in scale next to the park. Both need outdoor rooms.
rows.quote: Neither gives a family a verandah. B at least doesn't shout over the maidan.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A 133 m square rotated toward the sea and park, identical at every floor. There is no outdoor space for any flat, and it towers over the low heritage precinct around Shivaji Park.

floor_changes.direction: W corner, toward the Arabian Sea
floor_changes.amount: double-height verandahs 3 m deep on every flat
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space per flat and monsoon shade
Tempers the jump in scale next to the park

win1.whats_wrong: Lower at 97 m and turned slightly further, which sits better against the park edge. It is still a mute box without a single balcony.

floor_changes.why: Stepped verandahs give every flat a terrace facing the sea
Mehrotra-like engagement with the street

rows.reason: The two schemes look identical.
rows.quote: Same building twice. Give it a crown and a front door and we can talk.

hyb2.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon that rotates a few degrees as it rises. It is pleasant enough, but it sits pinched between large Canary Wharf slabs with nothing at street level, and the crown is flat.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.amount: sloping crown with 8 m of fall
floor_changes.why: Gives it an identity against the cluster

floor_changes.direction: toward the DLR and dock edge
floor_changes.why: Public realm

win1.whats_wrong: The same as A. The images are indistinguishable, so it has the same issues.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the S
floor_changes.why: Frees the faces from the adjacent towers to the NE

rows.reason: The rounded plates and banding give it a softer sculptural presence, but both designs share the same problem with the central tower.
